source_read: PMC HTML (PMC5760333), an author manuscript (NIHMS894998) of the Addiction article 113(2):257-265, not the publisher's version; read in full on 2026-10-31: Abstract, introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion with limitations and implications, Acknowledgments; Tables 1-5 read as text. Online supplement (Supplemental Tables 1-7) not read.

claims.overstatement: None. One imprecision: 'scored lower than the others on 4 of 6 executive-function scores' should be 'performed worse on'. One of the four is SWM Strategy, where higher scores are worse and the dependent group scored higher (0.21 against −0.01).
claims.note: Checked: 84 of 1,989 (4.2%) with past-year DSM-IV dependence at 18, against the 1,902 to 1,905 without; worse on 4 of 6 CANTAB scores (RVP A prime, SWM Strategy, Spatial Span Forward and Reversed) and on 2 (the spatial spans) after age-12 IQ; no differences in the 57 discordant pairs; Spatial Span Forward −0.48 against 0.02 in the full sample and −0.38 against −0.18 (t −1.30, p = .20) in the pairs; sex-adjusted z-scores. Worth adding: with frequency of use as the exposure, the twin who used more often did worse than the co-twin on Spatial Span Reversed (beta −0.07, p = .036; .022 after age-12 IQ; 974 pairs), the one within-pair difference, which the authors say may be a false positive. In the full sample, frequency went with worse performance on 5 of 6 tests after age-12 IQ. The tests cover attention/vigilance and spatial working memory only, with no memory tests. Use was mostly light (63% none in the past year, 28% less than monthly, 1% many times a day).

anchors.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 4
anchors.extracted: Sex-adjusted z-scores at 18, dependent (n = 83-84) against not dependent (n = 1,895-1,902): RVP A prime −0.22 against 0.02 (t −2.26, p = .024); SWM Strategy 0.21 against −0.01 (higher worse; t 2.40, p = .017); Spatial Span Forward −0.48 against 0.02 (t −4.57, p < .001); Spatial Span Reversed −0.33 against 0.01 (t −3.37, p < .001); RVP false alarms (p = .83) and SWM errors (p = .07) not different. After age-12 IQ only the spans differed: Forward −0.35 against 0.01 (t −3.60, p < .001), Reversed −0.20 against 0.01 (t −2.17, p = .030). In 56-57 discordant pairs no test differed, e.g., Spatial Span Forward −0.38 against −0.18 (t −1.30, p = .20).

anchors.locator: Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 5
anchors.extracted: Standardized beta per SD of past-year frequency, sex-adjusted. Full sample (n about 1,985): worse on 5 of 6 tests after age-12 IQ (e.g., Spatial Span Forward and Reversed −0.09, p < .001; RVP A prime −0.05, p = .020; RVP false alarms 0.01, p = .56). Within 967-974 twin pairs: only Spatial Span Reversed, −0.07 (p = .036; .022 after IQ); the others near zero (p .14 to .96).

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Executive Functions, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Past-year DSM-IV cannabis dependence at 18: n = 84 (4%); of 977 complete pairs, 908 concordant for no dependence, 12 concordant for dependence, 57 discordant. Past-year frequency at 18: never 63%, less than monthly 28%, monthly 3%, weekly 3%, daily 2%, many times a day 1%. Executive functions at 18 only: CANTAB tests of attention/vigilance and working memory, standardized to mean 0, SD 1.

Associations in the full sample were not seen within pairs; the authors call the within-pair Spatial Span Reversed result a possible false positive. Limitations: self-reported use without biological tests; no memory tests; discordant-pair analyses possibly underpowered; intense use (many times a day) rare at 1%.

claims.overstatement: None: the claim says IQ 'did not fall significantly more' and that discordant twins 'did not differ', with the editors' intervals, and does not adopt the authors' conclusion that short-term adolescent use 'does not appear to cause IQ decline'.
claims.note: All numbers check against Table 2 and Table 3: 1,989 tested at 5, 12 and 18; 84 against 1,905; sex-adjusted differences −5.23 (t −2.94, p = .003), −5.61 (t −3.11, p = .002) and −7.34 (t −5.27, p < .001); change 12 to 18, −1.81 against −0.08, difference −1.73 (t −1.27, p = .20); 57 discordant pairs: age 18 −1.45 (p = .42), change 0.05 (p = .98); frequency, change beta −0.05 (p = .035) and −0.02 within pairs (p = .46). The editors' intervals reproduce: −1.73 with SE 1.36 gives −4.4 to 0.9; −1.45 with SE 1.79 gives −5.0 to 2.1. Worth adding: 'IQ' here is a pro-rated estimate from two subtests (Vocabulary and Block Design at 5; Information and Matrix Reasoning at 12 and 18), standardized within the sample. The within-pair change estimate (0.05) has no interval, and its t is rounded to 0.02, so its precision cannot be recovered; with 57 pairs it cannot exclude a decline as large as the full-sample −1.73. After age-5 IQ, the full-sample change was −2.02 (t −1.49, p = .14). The frequency coefficients are standardized betas per SD of frequency, not IQ points. In the Discussion the authors describe their 2012 Dunedin finding as an 8-point decline 'from age 18-38', but the Dunedin baseline was childhood IQ at 7-13 (see the meier_2012 out file). That does not affect this claim.

anchors.extracted: E-Risk: 2,232 children in 1,116 families (93% of eligible) with same-sex twins born 1994-1995 in England and Wales, first seen at 5; 56% MZ; age-18 participation 93% (n = 2,066); no differences at 5 in SES, IQ or behaviour problems between those seen and not seen at 18. Analysed: 1,989 with IQ at 5, 12 and 18 (96% of those seen at 18); 47.3% male; past-year use 37.6%; dependence 4.2%.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Intelligence Quotient (IQ), 1st paragraph; Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: IQ at 5 (WPPSI-R short form: Vocabulary and Block Design, pro-rated), 12 (WISC-R) and 18 (WAIS-IV); at 12 and 18 the same two subtests (Information, Matrix Reasoning) give pro-rated IQ; scores standardized on the sample (mean 100, SD 15). Only 19 had tried cannabis by 12. Decline analysed from 12 to 18 (same subtests), with age-5 IQ as an added covariate; sex in all models; twin clustering handled with SURVEYREG.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 1st paragraph; Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Exposure: past-year DSM-IV cannabis dependence at 18 (n = 84, 4%). Of 977 complete pairs, 57 were discordant for dependence (908 concordant without, 12 concordant with). Co-twin analyses for dependence used the 57 discordant pairs; for frequency, within-pair difference scores in all 977 pairs, MZ and DZ combined.

Change 12 to 18: −0.08 against −1.81, difference −1.73 (t −1.27, p = .20); with age-5 IQ controlled, age 12 −2.80 (p = .08), age 18 −4.82 (p < .001), change −2.02 (t −1.49, p = .14). Editors' approximate 95% CI for −1.73: −4.4 to 0.9.

anchors.extracted: 57 pairs discordant for dependence, non-dependent twin against dependent co-twin: age 5 93.50 against 94.26 (0.76, p = .70); age 12 95.47 against 93.97 (−1.50, p = .43); age 18 94.31 against 92.86 (−1.45, t −0.81, p = .42; editors' approximate CI −5.0 to 2.1); change −1.16 against −1.11 (0.05, t 0.02, p = .98). Both twins in discordant pairs scored below the norm, which the authors read as family confounding. Similar after excluding the 19 who had tried cannabis by 12 (Supplemental Table 3, not read).

Full sample: age 5 −0.05 (p = .07), age 12 −0.11 and age 18 −0.15 (both p < .001), change 12 to 18 −0.05 (p = .035; −0.05, p = .023 with age-5 IQ). Within 977 pairs: 0.02 (p = .56), 0.03 (p = .32), 0.00 (p = .94), change −0.02 (p = .46). Weekly use against none: little evidence of greater decline (Supplemental Table 6, not read).

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; 5th paragraph (limitations); Abstract › Conclusions
anchors.extracted: The authors conclude that relatively short-term adolescent use does not appear to cause IQ decline even at the level of dependence, and that family background explains the lower scores. They say this does not conflict with the Dunedin persistent-use finding, and that more research is needed on gradual impairment in longer-term persistent use. Limitations: self-report; discordant-pair analyses possibly underpowered (effect sizes near zero); intense use rare (1%).

Recomputed: within pairs −0.20 (SE 0.154) gives −0.51 to 0.11; full sample −0.50 (SE 0.109) gives −0.71 to −0.29.
In the PMC text the false-positive remark and the limitations share the Discussion's 5th paragraph.
The finding paraphrases the Discussion accurately; what the Discussion says about Dunedin is itself inaccurate (see reporting issue 4).

reporting_issues.note: The wording is not merely ambiguous; it is wrong on two points. (1) The Discussion says the decline was 'from age 18–38', but Meier et al. (2012) measured IQ change from childhood (mean of ages 7-13) to 38 and had no IQ test at 18 (Meier 2012, Methods › Statistical Analysis). (2) It says that people dependent only at 18 'did not show IQ decline'. In Meier 2012 Fig. 2, the matching group (dependence before 18 at one wave, n = 17) changed by about −0.22 SD (about 3 points), not significantly different from adult onset (p = .44); no test against no change is reported. The 8 points refers to the 23 adolescent-onset people with dependence at 3 or more waves, read from a figure. Suggested issue text: the Discussion misstates the time frame and the single-wave result of the 2012 Dunedin paper; take Dunedin figures from Meier et al. (2012) itself.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns overall, judged for the within-pair estimates, with no domain high. The main limit on the null results is imprecision rather than bias, which the card states, and GRADE should take it up under imprecision. The full-sample comparisons that the claims also cite (lower IQ at 5 and 12; change −1.73) are adjusted only for sex; that is acceptable for describing pre-existing differences.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is acceptable given the stated limits. The abstract's 'Family background factors explain why adolescent cannabis users perform worse' states as established what rests on 57 pooled MZ/DZ discordant pairs, with no intervals and with non-shared confounders unmeasured; 'are consistent with family background explaining' would match the data.
